q: 101. D10 of the soil is the diameter in mm such that ...........
options: 10% of the soil is coarser than this value
10% of the soil is finer than this value
this value has no bearing on particle size distribution
explain: D10 represents the 'effective size'; it means 10% of the soil particles by weight are smaller (finer) than this specific diameter.

q: 102. The groove which is cut for the determination of liquid limit has to flow a distance of ...........
explain: In the Casagrande liquid limit test, the soil is considered to have reached the limit when the two halves of the cake flow together for a distance of 12 mm (approx. 0.5 inch).

q: 103. The drop of the cup for the liquid limit determination is ...........
explain: The Casagrande apparatus is calibrated so that the brass cup drops exactly 10 mm (1 cm) onto the hard rubber base.

q: 104. At liquid limit a soil has ...........
options: nothing to do with shear strength
explain: All soils at their liquid limit possess a very small, uniform shear strength (approximately 1.7 to 2.0 kN/m²).

q: 105. When the plastic limit cannot be determined, the soil is reported to be ...........
explain: Soils like clean sands that cannot be rolled into 3mm threads are classified as non-plastic (NP).

q: 106. A soil consisting of approximately equal percentage of sand, silt and clay is referred to as ...........
explain: Loam is a specific textural classification for a soil that contains a balanced mixture of sand, silt, and clay.

q: 107. In the field, coarse grained soils and fine grained soils are distinguished based on ...........
options: appearance of individual grains to the naked eye
explain: Coarse-grained soils (sand/gravel) have grains visible to the naked eye, whereas fine-grained soils (silt/clay) do not.

q: 108. In the field, sand can be distinguished from silt by ...........
explain: The dispersion test (dropping soil into water) helps distinguish sand, which settles quickly, from silt, which stays in suspension longer.

q: 109. Shaking test is also called as ...........
explain: Dilatancy (or shaking) test involves observing the reaction of a wet soil pat when shaken in the palm; it helps identify silts.

q: 110. In the field, Dilatancy test is used to differentiate clay from ...........
explain: Silts show a quick reaction (dilatant) to shaking, while clays show a slow or no reaction.

q: 111. Toughness test is also called as ...........
explain: The rolling test (creating 3mm threads) is used to assess the toughness and plasticity of the soil near the plastic limit.

q: 112. In the field, Rolling test is used to differentiate clay from ...........
explain: Clays can be rolled into thin threads at the plastic limit, whereas silts are brittle and crumble easily.

q: 113. For classification purposes, coarse grained soils shall be divided into following number of sub-divisions ...........
explain: Coarse-grained soils are primarily subdivided into two groups: Gravels (G) and Sands (S).

q: 114. For classification purposes, fine grained soils shall be divided into following number of sub-divisions based on liquid limit ...........
explain: Fine-grained soils are divided into three: Low compressibility (LL < 35), Intermediate (35-50), and High (LL > 50).

q: 115. The coarse grained soils will lie on boundary classification when they have this percentage of fines ...........
explain: Dual symbols (e.g., GW-GC) are required for coarse soils containing between 5% and 12% fines.

q: 116. The basis for the classification of the fine grained soils is ...........
explain: The Plasticity Chart (A-line chart) is the standard tool for classifying silts and clays based on their Plasticity Index and Liquid Limit.

q: 117. A reduction of liquid limit after oven drying to a value less than three-fourth of the liquid limit before oven-drying is an indication of ...........
explain: Organic soils show a significant drop in Liquid Limit (often > 25%) when oven-dried compared to their natural state.

q: 118. Soils which plot above the A-line, and which have a plasticity Index between 4 to 7 are classified as ...........
explain: The 'dual symbol' zone on the plasticity chart is for soils with PI between 4 and 7 and LL between roughly 12-25.

q: 119. According to I.S. classification, the value of liquid limit for fine grained soils of high compressibility is ...........
explain: Soils with a Liquid Limit greater than 50% are categorized as highly compressible (indicated by the suffix 'H').

q: 120. Specific surface of the following soil is more ...........
explain: Clays have the smallest particle size and flaky shapes, resulting in the highest surface area per unit mass (specific surface).

q: 121. The dry density of soil can be defined as the ratio of ...........
options: weight of solids to the total volume of the soil
weight of the soil to the volume of the soil
unit weight of the soil to the unit weight of water
explain: Dry density (ρd) is mass of solids divided by total volume; dry unit weight (γd) is weight of solids divided by total volume.

q: 122. A pycnometer is used to determine ...........
explain: The pycnometer is a standard laboratory vessel used specifically to find specific gravity and, if G is known, the water content.

q: 123. The thickness of adsorbed layers of soil is measured in ...........
explain: Adsorbed water layers on clay particles are extremely thin, typically measured in Angstroms (10^-10 meters).

q: 124. Three phase diagram of soil represents ...........
options: dust, fine sand and coarse sand
explain: A standard soil phase diagram models the three constituents: solid particles, liquid (water), and gas (air).

q: 125. If the water content of a fully saturated soil mass is 100%, then the voids ratio will be ...........
options: less than specific gravity of soil
equal to specific gravity of soil
greater than specific gravity of soil
independent of specific gravity of soil
explain: Using Se = wG: if S=1 (saturated) and w=1 (100%), then e = 1 * G, so void ratio equals specific gravity.

q: 126. Plasticity index is obtained as the difference between ...........
explain: Plasticity Index (PI) = LL - PL. It represents the range of water content over which the soil behaves plastically.

q: 127. The ratio of plasticity index to clay fraction is known as ...........
explain: Activity (A) = PI / (% clay particles). It indicates the swelling potential and mineralogical activity of the clay.

q: 128. Two soils A and B: LL (A: 40%, B: 60%), PL (A: 20%, B: 25%). Which soil is more plastic?
explain: PI for A = 40-20 = 20. PI for B = 60-25 = 35. Soil B has a higher Plasticity Index, so it is more plastic.

q: 129. The slope of the flow curve obtained in liquid limit test is called ...........
explain: The flow index (If) is the slope of the flow curve (water content vs. log of blows) and represents the rate of loss of shear strength.

q: 130. The ratio of plasticity index to flow index is called ...........
explain: Toughness Index (It) = PI / If. It gives an indication of the shear strength of the soil at the plastic limit.

q: 131. Two soils P and Q have toughness index 4 and 10. Which soil has better strength at plastic limit?
explain: Higher toughness index indicates higher shear strength at the plastic limit.

q: 132. Rock flour is the name of ...........
explain: Rock flour consists of fine-grained particles of rock (inorganic silt) produced by glacial grinding.

q: 133. With reference to shrinkage and swelling, the most active clay mineral is ...........
explain: Montmorillonite has a large specific surface and weak interlayer bonds, allowing water to enter easily and cause massive swelling/shrinkage.

q: 134. In a soil if the water content is equal to the liquid limit, its relative consistency is ...........
explain: Consistency Index (Ic) = (LL - w) / PI. If w = LL, then Ic = (LL - LL) / PI = 0.

q: 135. The difference between plastic limit and shrinkage limit is called ...........
explain: Shrinkage Index (SI) = PL - SL. It represents the range of water content in the semi-solid state.

q: 136. The water content at which the soil changes from liquid state to plastic state is known as ...........
explain: The Liquid Limit (LL) is the boundary water content between the liquid and plastic states.

q: 137. Deforming soil rapidly without volume change, rupture or elastic rebound is termed as ...........
explain: Plasticity is the unique property of clay-water systems that allows permanent deformation without cracking.

q: 138. The liquidity index is given as ...........
explain: Liquidity Index (Il) = (w - PL) / PI. It indicates the proximity of the natural water content to the liquid limit.

q: 139. Velocity with which a soil grain settles out of suspension depends upon ...........
explain: Per Stoke's Law, settling velocity is influenced by particle diameter (size), density (weight), and drag (shape).

q: 140. Degree of saturation of soil is generally ...........
explain: Saturation (S) is the percentage of void space filled with water, naturally ranging from 0 (dry) to 100 (saturated).

q: 141. Thixotropy of soils refers to ...........
options: gain of strength with time after remoulding
loss of strength with time after remoulding
thickening of soil with particles with water
explain: Thixotropy is the property of some clays to regain a portion of their lost strength over time at a constant water content after being disturbed.

q: 142. Ratio of compressive strength of undisturbed clay to remoulded state is ...........
explain: This ratio is called Sensitivity. For almost all clays, the undisturbed strength is significantly higher than the remoulded strength, so the ratio > 1.

q: 143. The basis for all soil classification system is ...........
explain: Standard systems (USCS, IS) use particle size distribution (for coarse soils) and Atterberg limits (for fine soils) as the primary criteria.

q: 144. Property of soil which allows water to flow through the soil is known as ...........
explain: Permeability (or hydraulic conductivity) is the measure of the ease with which water can flow through the pore spaces of a soil.

q: 145. Velocity of flow through porous medium is directly proportional to hydraulic gradient is ...........
explain: Darcy’s Law (v = ki) states that the discharge velocity is proportional to the hydraulic gradient in laminar flow.

q: 146. Darcy's law is applicable if a soil is ...........
explain: Classic Darcy flow assumes a homogeneous, isotropic, and incompressible medium with fully saturated laminar flow.

q: 147. According to Darcy's law, the flow velocity can be obtained by ...........
explain: The discharge velocity (v) is equal to the coefficient of permeability (k) times the hydraulic gradient (i).

q: 148. Coefficient of percolation and coefficient of permeability are related by ...........
explain: Since seepage velocity (vs) = v / n, the coefficient of percolation (Kp) = k / n, where n is porosity.

q: 149. Coefficient of percolation has a value ...........
options: less than the coefficient of permeability
equal to the coefficient of permeability
explain: Because porosity (n) is always less than 1, dividing k by n (Kp = k/n) results in a value larger than k.

q: 150. Constant of proportionality between seepage velocity and hydraulic gradient is ...........
explain: The coefficient of percolation (Kp) is specifically associated with the actual seepage velocity through the pores, not the superficial discharge velocity.

q: 151. Capillary force is dependent on ............
explain: Capillary force is primarily driven by the surface tension of water and the size of the soil pores. Surface tension creates the pressure difference necessary for water to rise against gravity.

q: 152. The zone of soil mass above the water table which is saturated by capillary moisture is called ............
explain: The capillary fringe is the subsurface layer in which groundwater seeps up from a water table by capillary action to fill pores, creating a saturated zone above the phreatic surface.

q: 153. The number of heads that are used for defining the water head at a point in a soil mass are ............
explain: In soil mechanics, the total head at a point consists of three components: Datum (elevation) head, Pressure head, and Velocity head (though velocity head is often negligible).

q: 154. Velocity head in soils will be ............
explain: Due to the very low velocity of water flow through the small pores of soil, the term $v^2/2g$ (velocity head) is extremely small and is generally neglected in calculations.

q: 155. The pore water pressure in the capillary zone is ............
explain: Water in the capillary zone is under tension (suction), which is represented mathematically as negative pore water pressure relative to atmospheric pressure.

q: 156. Water which the soil particles freely adsorb from atmosphere by the physical forces of attraction, and is held by the force of adhesion is known as ............
explain: Hygroscopic water is the moisture absorbed from the atmosphere that forms a very thin film around soil particles, held so tightly by adhesion that it cannot move under gravity.

q: 157. Capillary water is held in the interstices of soil due to capillarity forces. The capillary forces depends upon ............
explain: Capillary rise is governed by the formula $h = 4\sigma\cos	heta / (\gamma_w d)$. Thus, it depends on surface tension ($\sigma$), pore size (diameter $d$), and the resulting pressure differences.

q: 158. Out of the following, which will have the maximum value of surface tension forces ............
explain: Mercury has a significantly higher surface tension (approximately 480 mN/m) compared to water (72 mN/m) and other common liquids due to strong metallic bonding.

q: 159. A soil which does not permit the passage or seepage of any permeant through its voids, is known as ............
explain: Impermeable soil (like dense clay) has such low hydraulic conductivity that it effectively prevents the flow of water through its pore spaces.

q: 160. In most of the practical flow problems in soil mechanics, the flow is ............
explain: Because the flow velocity in soils is typically very low and the pore channels are narrow, the Reynolds number remains small, ensuring the flow is laminar (obeying Darcy's Law).

q: 161. The velocity of percolation is defined as ............
options: the discharge per unit of gross c/s area
the discharge per unit of net c/s area
the discharge per unit of total c/s area
explain: The velocity of percolation ($v_s$) is the actual speed of water moving through the voids (net cross-sectional area), whereas the discharge velocity ($v$) assumes flow through the entire gross area.

q: 162. Magnitude of capillary rise is more in ............
explain: Capillary rise is inversely proportional to the pore diameter. Since clays have the smallest pore sizes among the listed soils, they exhibit the highest capillary rise.

q: 163. The height to which water can be lifted by capillarity is ............
options: independent of the atmospheric pressure value
depends upon the atmospheric pressure value
increases with decreasing diameter of the passage and is independent of the atmospheric pressure
explain: Capillary rise is a surface tension phenomenon governed by the Jurin's Law formula $h =  rac{4\sigma\cos	heta}{\gamma_w d}$, which shows it depends on pore diameter ($d$) but is independent of external atmospheric pressure.

q: 164. Piping in soils is due to ............
options: erosion of subsoil by high velocity of seepage flow
leakage of water through pipes laid in dams
passage of water through well-connected pores in soil
explain: Piping occurs when the exit gradient exceeds the critical gradient, causing seepage forces to erode and transport soil particles, creating a 'pipe-like' hollow through the soil mass.

q: 165. Permeability of soil varies ............
options: inversely as square of grain size
explain: According to Allen Hazen's formula, $k = C \cdot (D_{10})^2$, the coefficient of permeability ($k$) is directly proportional to the square of the effective grain size ($D_{10}$).

q: 166. Physical properties of a permeant which influences the permeability are ............
explain: The theoretical equation for permeability $k =  rac{D^2 \gamma_w}{\mu}  rac{e^3}{1+e}$ shows that $k$ is directly proportional to the unit weight ($\gamma_w$) and inversely proportional to the dynamic viscosity ($\mu$) of the fluid.

q: 167. The permeability is ............
options: Directly proportional to unit weight, inversely proportional to viscosity
Directly proportional to viscosity, inversely proportional to unit weight
Directly proportional to both unit weight and viscosity
Inversely proportional to both unit weight and viscosity
explain: As per the fundamental permeability equation, higher unit weight increases flow due to gravity, while higher viscosity resists flow, creating an inverse relationship with viscosity.

q: 168. Due to rise in temperature, the unit weight and viscosity of the permeant fluid are reduced to 90% and 60% respectively. If other things remain constant, the coefficient of permeability ............
explain: Since $k \propto \gamma / \mu$, the new permeability $k' = k \cdot (0.9 / 0.6) = 1.5k$. This represents a 50% increase.

q: 169. Units of co-efficient of permeability ............
explain: Coefficient of permeability has the dimensions of velocity ($L/T$), commonly expressed in cm/sec or m/day.

q: 170. Coefficient of permeability of a soil ............
options: increases with the decrease in temperature
increases with the increase in temperature
explain: An increase in temperature reduces the viscosity of water, which in turn increases the soil's permeability.

q: 171. Void ratio of soil 'A' = 0.80, Void ratio of soil 'B' = 1.20. Which soil is more pervious?
explain: Permeability increases with the void ratio. Therefore, soil B, with a higher void ratio (1.20), is more pervious than soil A (0.80).

q: 172. A sand has e= 0.8 and another clay has e = 1.2, which is more pervious?
explain: Although the clay has a higher void ratio, sand is more pervious because its individual pores are much larger and more interconnected compared to the microscopic, poorly connected pores in clay.

q: 173. The coefficient of permeability is proportional to void ratio as ............
explain: The most widely accepted relationship (from the Kozeny-Carman equation) states that permeability is proportional to the function $ rac{e^3}{1+e}$.

q: 174. Which of the following soils has largest permeability?
explain: Gravel has the largest grain size and largest interconnected voids, resulting in the highest coefficient of permeability among the options.

q: 175. The coefficient grain size of soil (D10) is 0.3 mm, the value of coefficient of permeability as per Hazen is (coefficient of Hazen C = 10) ............
explain: Using Hazen's formula $k = C \cdot (D_{10})^2$, where $k$ is in cm/s and $D_{10}$ is in cm: $k = 100 \cdot (0.03)^2 = 0.09 	ext{ cm/s} = 0.9 	ext{ mm/sec}$.

q: 176. Falling head permeameter is preferable when soil sample is ............
explain: The falling head test is suited for fine-grained soils (like clay) with low permeability, where the small quantity of water passing through can be measured accurately by the drop in the standpipe.

q: 177. In the case of stratified soils, the permeability's Kx and Kz along and across stratification are related as ............
options: no relation between Kx and Kz
explain: In stratified deposits, the equivalent permeability parallel to the layers ($K_x$) is always greater than the equivalent permeability perpendicular to the layers ($K_z$).

q: 178. The range of coefficient of permeability of clay is about ............
explain: Clay is considered practically impervious, with a coefficient of permeability typically less than $10^{-6}$ cm/sec (often reaching $10^{-9}$ cm/sec).

q: 179. The value of coefficient of permeability of sand is ............
explain: Clean sand generally falls within the permeability range of $1$ to $10^{-2}$ cm/sec.

q: 180. Soils with a value for coefficient of permeability ranging between 10⁻⁴ to 10⁻⁶ are classified as ............
explain: Soils with $k$ values between $10^{-4}$ and $10^{-6}$ cm/sec are termed semi-pervious (typical for silts and silty sands).

q: 181. The presence of entrapped air in a soil will ............
explain: Entrapped air bubbles block the pore channels, effectively reducing the area available for water flow and thus decreasing permeability.

q: 182. The presence of organic matter in a soil will ............
explain: Organic matter tends to fill and block pore spaces and may promote compaction, leading to a decrease in the overall permeability of the soil.

q: 183. The hydraulic head that would produce a quick condition in a sand stratum of thickness 1.5 m and of specific gravity 2.67 and void ratio of 0.67 is equal to ............
explain: The critical gradient $i_c = (G-1)/(1+e) = (2.67-1)/(1+0.67) = 1.0$. The required head $h = i_c \cdot L = 1.0 \cdot 1.5 = 1.5 	ext{ m}$.

q: 184. A critical hydraulic gradient occurs when ............
options: seepage pressure is in upward direction
explain: A critical gradient occurs during upward flow when the seepage force exactly balances the buoyant weight of the soil, resulting in zero effective stress.

q: 185. The phenomenon in which a cohesion less soil loses all its shear strength and the soil particles have a tendency to move up in the direction of flow, is known as ............
explain: These terms are used interchangeably to describe the state where seepage forces eliminate effective stress in non-cohesive soils, causing them to behave like a liquid.

q: 186. Quick sand is ............
options: a condition in which cohesion is decreased quickly
a sand which can act as a quick filter
condition in which cohesion less soil loses its shear strength due to the upward flow of water
explain: Quick sand is not a type of sand but a hydraulic condition where upward seepage pressure equals the submerged weight of the soil, nullifying shear strength.

q: 187. The quantity of seepage in a soil is ............
options: directly proportional to the coefficient of permeability
inversely proportional to the coefficient of permeability
directly proportional to the uniformity coefficient of the soil
explain: According to Darcy's Law ($Q = kiA$), the seepage quantity is directly proportional to the coefficient of permeability ($k$).

q: 188. Flow net consists of a number of stream lines and equipotential lines which are ............
explain: In an isotropic soil, flow lines and equipotential lines intersect at right angles ($90^\circ$), forming an orthogonal grid.

q: 189. The seepage force in a soil is ............
explain: Seepage force acts in the direction of flow (along flow lines), which is always perpendicular to the lines of equal potential (equipotential lines).

q: 190. The seepage force in soils at exit is proportional to ............
options: the head of water at d/s
the head of water at u/s
explain: The seepage force per unit volume is $\gamma_w \cdot i$. At the exit point of a flow net, the force is directly proportional to the exit hydraulic gradient.

q: 191. Flow net is used for the determination of ............
explain: Flow nets are versatile tools used to calculate seepage quantity, pore water pressure (hydrostatic pressure), and exit gradients for stability analysis.

q: 192. Electrical analogy method is used to ............
options: find the depth to water table
find the water content in a soil
explain: Electrical analogy uses the similarity between Darcy's law and Ohm's law to model seepage and construct flow nets for complex boundary conditions.

q: 193. The shape factor of a flownet is defined as ............
explain: Shape factor ($N_f / N_d$) is the ratio of the number of flow channels to the number of equipotential drops, which is a constant for a given boundary geometry.

q: 194. The u/s face of an earth dam is ............
explain: The upstream face of a dam is submerged and in contact with water of the same potential, making it the first equipotential line ($100\%$ head).

q: 195. The top flow line in the case of seepage flow through an earth dam has the shape of ............
explain: According to Casagrande's solution, the phreatic line (top flow line) in an earth dam is approximately a base parabola.

q: 196. Flow through an earth dam is a case of ............
explain: It is unconfined flow because the top boundary of the flow (the phreatic line) is at atmospheric pressure and is not fixed by an impermeable boundary.

q: 197. The phreatic line is ............
options: the u/s face of the earth dam
d/s face of the earth dam
explain: The phreatic line is the seepage line that marks the upper boundary of the saturated zone; it is the top flow line where pressure is atmospheric.

q: 198. The hydrostatic pressure on the phreatic line with in a dam section is ............
explain: By definition, the phreatic line is the locus of points where the pore water pressure is zero (equal to atmospheric pressure).

q: 199. If h is the head of water stored, Nf is the number of flow lines and Nd is the number of equipotential drops in a flow net, then the seepage flow rate is given by ............
explain: The standard discharge formula from a flow net is $q = k \cdot H \cdot (N_f / N_d)$, where $H$ is the total head causing flow.

q: 200. The modified co-efficient of permeability k' in the case of an anisotropic soil is given by ............
explain: To analyze anisotropic soils, the coordinates are transformed, and the equivalent (modified) coefficient of permeability is taken as the geometric mean: $\sqrt{k_x \cdot k_z}$.
